analysis.one_liner: Limits how long a ticketing company can hold an exclusive contract to sell a venue's tickets.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: after being introduced in April 2023, it sat in the Senate Judiciary Committee until the Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: Large venues sign long-term exclusive contracts letting one ticketing company handle all initial ticket sales. This bill directs the Federal Trade Commission to cap the length of those exclusive deals, defining any contract longer than four years as 'excessive,' and to enforce the cap as an unfair method of competition with civil penalties. The point is to open ticketing to competition, which supporters argue would lower fees and improve service for fans. The bill never advanced beyond a Senate committee.
analysis.who_benefits: People who buy tickets to concerts, sports, theater, and comedy shows, who currently pay fees set in a market where one company holds exclusive contracts with most large venues; competing ticketing companies would also gain a chance to win venue business [S2][S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Concertgoers, sports fans, and competing ticketing firms

how_it_helps.text: Bars a primary ticketing provider from holding an exclusive contract to sell essentially all of a large venue's (5,000+ capacity) tickets for an 'excessive' length of time, which the FTC must set at more than four years [S2][S3].
Enforces the limit through the FTC as an unfair method of competition, with civil penalties designed to deter violations and capped at the size of the affected commerce [S3].
Leaves existing antitrust laws fully intact, adding a new enforcement tool rather than replacing existing ones [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The dominant primary ticketing company, whose long exclusive venue contracts are the target, and venues that profit from locking in a single ticketing partner for years at a time; fans would pay any transition costs only indirectly, if at all [S2][S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: The dominant ticketing company and locked-in venues

drawbacks.text: The bill does not ban exclusive contracts outright: the FTC's rules must treat anything up to four years as acceptable, so a company could still lock in every major venue contract of four years or more [S2][S3].
It targets only the length of exclusivity, not ticket fees, resale practices, or hidden charges, so fans' actual ticket costs may not fall much even with more competition [S2].
Its effect depends entirely on FTC rulemaking and enforcement, which could define 'excessive duration' loosely or enforce weakly [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: A modest, well-targeted pro-competition measure: it would not guarantee cheaper tickets, since it only shortens the leash on exclusive contracts rather than eliminating them or regulating fees, but the cost of trying is low and falls on the dominant ticketing firm and venue partners. Its main weakness is how much it leaves to the FTC's discretion.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee in April 2023, and the committee never took it up before the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Sen. Amy Klobuchar introduced the bill with Sen. Richard Blumenthal as its only cosponsor on April 26, 2023 [S3][S4].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on the Judiciary the same day; that is the last action in its history [S5].
No hearing, markup, floor vote, or companion House action appears in the record, and the Congress ended on January 3, 2025 [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The dominant ticketing company and its venue partners, who keep their long exclusive contracts because the bill died in committee without a vote.

for.name: Sen. Amy Klobuchar
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the Judiciary Committee; took no further procedural step recorded before the Congress ended.

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Sen. Dick Durbin (D-IL)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral on April 26, 2023 and never reported it out; no markup, hearing on the bill, or floor scheduling followed before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: Only two Democratic senators put their names on the bill and no vote or recorded opposition exists, so the partisan shape of the opposition cannot be read from the record [S4][S5].

industries.note: The bill aims squarely at long exclusive venue contracts of the kind the dominant ticketing platform holds with major arenas and stadiums; losing or shortening them opens its core market to rivals. Fans currently face fees and service quality set in a market where these exclusive deals are the norm.

industries.industry: Large concert and sports venues (5,000+ capacity)
industries.note: Venues could no longer sign one ticketing partner for long stretches, giving up guaranteed upfront payments and administrative simplicity from exclusivity. In exchange they would gain competing bids, which proponents argue would mean lower service fees and better terms for the venue and its customers.
